title: The useless tree
hookLine: a giant oak survives every axe because its wood is good for nothing (Zhuangzi 4)

cards: How was your week? Busy? Productive?
It's easy to measure a life by use. What got done. What it's good for.

Even rest gets sold as a way to be more productive later. In the book of Zhuangzi, a master carpenter named Shi is traveling with his apprentice, and they pass a village shrine with the biggest tree anyone has ever seen.
An oak, the translators usually say, wide enough to shade thousands of oxen. Crowds come just to stare at it. And the master carpenter walks right past without a glance.

teach.h: A BOAT SINKS, A COFFIN ROTS.
teach.b: The apprentice runs to catch up. Master, I've never seen timber like that. Why didn't you even look?
And the carpenter says: forget it. That tree's worthless. Make a boat from it, and it sinks.
A coffin, and it rots. A tool, and it breaks. A door, and it oozes sap.
A pillar, and the worms get in. That's why it's grown so old.

teach.h: THE TREE SPEAKS IN A DREAM.
teach.b: That night, the tree appears to the carpenter in a dream, and it's not pleased. What were you comparing me to, it asks?
The useful trees? The pear, the orange, the ones with fruit? The moment their fruit is ripe, they're stripped and their branches torn.
Their usefulness makes their life bitter, and they don't live out their years. I've been working at being useless for a very long time, the tree says, and it has been of great use to me.
If I'd been useful, would I ever have grown this big? The chapter ends with a line people still quote: everyone knows the usefulness of the useful.
Nobody knows the usefulness of the useless. Zhuangzi isn't telling anyone to stop working. He's poking at a habit of mind: judging everything, including people, by what it produces.
The tree's shade, its shelter, the crowds who come to stand under it: none of that counts as use, to the carpenter.
But it's why the tree is still alive, and why people travel to see it. Some of what matters most in a life is useless in exactly this way.

how: Taoist tradition reads the useless tree as a teaching about the value of what can't be measured, and the Zhuangzi returns to useless trees several times, including in its first and fourth chapters.

o: the old sage said to have written the Tao Te Ching
a Chinese carpenter who spared an old oak
an ancient Chinese thinker of playful stories

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: had never seen timber like it
stripped, and don't live out their years

s: the carpenter admired the tree's timber
he called it worthless: boats sink, coffins rot, doors ooze sap.
the tree speaks to the carpenter in a dream
and asks what he was comparing it to.
Zhuangzi is telling people to stop working
he's poking at the habit of judging everything, and everyone, by what it produces.

games.q: you're the old tree. a carpenter has just called you worthless. what do you say when you visit his dream?
o: prove him wrong: list your uses.
being useless is what kept me alive.
agree, and wish you'd been a fruit tree.
games.why: the tree says the useful trees are stripped and die young. if I'd been useful, would I have grown this big?

practice: Sit like a big old tree nobody wants for timber: don't try to get better at anything, don't relax so you'll be more productive later, and let the breath come and go on its own.
If a to-do thought appears, let it pass like a carpenter walking by. You're not here for anything; you're just alive.

wordCard.voice: Zhuangzi. The ancient thinker whose useless oak, unwanted by any carpenter, lived long enough to shelter everyone.

orig.note: Chinese, wú yòng zhī yòng: the usefulness of the useless, the phrase that closes Zhuangzi chapter four.

carryVoice: Your line: useless, and alive. The tree worked hard at being useless. See you on the bridge tomorrow.
